title: 'Black Swan' investor predicts AI boom ends with crash of a lifetime
excerpt: Universa Investments' Mark Spitznagel told BI that he expects one more "euphoric rally" followed by a "bigger crash than we've seen in our lifetime."
content_html:
'Black Swan' investor Mark Spitznagel says the crash of a lifetime is coming after one more 'euphoric rally'

By Theron Mohamed

You're currently following this author! Want to unfollow? Unsubscribe via the link in your email.

Mark Spitznagel says the AI boom likely has further to run, but a monumental crash is coming.

The founder and chief of Universa Investments, a "Black Swan" fund that aims to win big from catastrophes, shared his stock-market outlook and reflected on his investing style in a recent interview with Business Insider.

Spitznagel said Universa's signature tail-hedging strategy has enabled him to be "extremely bullish" for the past four years, despite his hedge fund being "certainly the most bearish vehicle you'll ever find."

He flagged signs of excessive leverage and "hubristic, humongous bets," but said he didn't see anything likely to cause an imminent stock-market crash.

However, he warned the economy is "rolling over" as the aftershocks from interest-rate hikes in recent years haven't yet fully materialized.

Spitznagel said that Michael Burry, the investor of "The Big Short" fame, is right to worry about AI hyperscalers' overinvestment in microchips and data centers, circular financing deals, and hidden liabilities. Yet Burry is "going to get the timing wrong," he said.

"I will be the biggest bear that you'll hear from in the months ahead," Spitznagel said. "I'm just not right now."

He predicted "one more really big, risk-on, insane, euphoric rally to come across risk assets."

"But once that's over, and it could be sooner than later, I think we're going to get a bigger crash than we've seen in our lifetime," he added.

Tough trading

"It's like you're playing the piano for 10 years and you still can't play 'Chopsticks,' and the only thing you have to keep you going is the belief that one day you'll wake up and play like Rachmaninoff."

That's how Spitznagel described his investing approach to journalist Malcolm Gladwell for a 2002 article in The New Yorker. Spitznagel was then head trader at Empirica Capital, a hedge fund he launched with "The Black Swan" author Nassim Taleb in 1999.

The pair specialized in protecting portfolios against extreme, rare, and unpredictable events. Their approach meant losing money on almost every trading day, as they wagered the huge gains they'd reap when disaster eventually struck would more than offset the day-to-day pain.

"It's the hardest thing," Spitznagel — who left the now-defunct Empirica to launch Universa in 2007 — told Business Insider. Taleb serves as Universa's scientific advisor.

The psychological and structural difficulty of chasing large, lumpy returns instead of modest, regular gains is a big part of the appeal to Spitznagel.

"One way to have real alpha is to go after a return stream, or a type of payoff, literally nobody else wants to do," he said.

Universa's signature tail-hedging strategy — which centers on buying "out-of-the-money" options that pay off if prices move dramatically — returned 4,144% in the first quarter of 2020, when the COVID-19 pandemic tanked markets.

Spitznagel told his clients at the time that if they'd allocated 3.3% of their portfolio to Universa and the rest to an S&P 500 tracker fund, they would have been in the green in March, whereas the index was down 12%.

By allocating a small amount to Universa, investors can make their portfolios less risky while also boosting their returns, Spitznagel told Business Insider.

They can be more bullish knowing they won't blow up, and when Universa's insurance-style hedge pays off in a crash, they can take those gains and reinvest them to capitalize on a subsequent rally, he said.

Spitznagel drew a parallel to Warren Buffett using insurance float — the funds left over after his insurance companies collected premiums and paid out claims — to scoop up bargains during market downturns, as he famously did during the 2008 financial crisis.

塞隆·穆罕默德是《商业内幕》国际团队驻伦敦记者。 他的报道领域涵盖金融、投资、财富、市场和经济。Theron 于 2019 年加入 BI，担任 Markets Insider 的记者，并晋升为通讯员，然后转到趋势团队，然后是更广泛的国际团队。 他此前曾为《投资者纪事》杂志报道科技、媒体和电信股票，并曾在《金融时报》数据团队短暂任职。 他在纽约《华尔街日报》实习，主要为《Heard on the Street》撰稿。塞隆曾为《独立报》、《电讯报》、《连线》和几家小型出版物担任自由撰稿人。 他拥有伦敦经济学院地理学学士学位和哥伦比亚大学新闻学硕士学位。塞隆经常报道沃伦·巴菲特、迈克尔·伯里等精英投资者。 他还撰写有关世界上最富有的人的文章，并分享各种富有和成功人士的财务建议。向塞隆发送电子邮件至 tmohamed@businessinsider.com，并在 X @theron_mohamed 上关注他。
